# Prospective multi-pathogen disease forecasting using autonomous LLM-guided tree search

**Authors:** Sarah Martinson Affiliation: Google Research Affiliation: School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University Michael P. Brenner Affiliation: Google Research Affiliation: School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University Martyna Plomecka Affiliation: Google Deepmind Brian P. Williams Affiliation: Google Research Nicholas G. Reich Affiliation: Google Research Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Amherst Zahra Shamsi Affiliation: Google Research

## Abstract

Probabilistic forecasting of infectious diseases is crucial for public health monitoring and preparedness but has historically relied on labor-intensive manual model curation by expert modeling teams. Bespoke development is an obstacle to scaling models to granular geographic resolutions or emerging pathogens. Here, we present an autonomous system—Empirical Research Assistance (ERA)—using Large Language Model-guided tree search to iteratively generate, evaluate, and optimize executable forecasting software. Mostly, ERA was provided the kernel of methods to implement, and in a few instances it was given license to develop ideas from scratch. In a fully prospective, real-time evaluation during the 2025–26 United States respiratory season, ERA generated methodologically diverse models for influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Aggregating a selection of these automatically-generated models yielded an ensemble that ranked first overall in official Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) post-season evaluations and outperformed the gold-standard CDC forecast ensembles across all three pathogens in a real-time prediction challenge. Additionally, ERA successfully navigated data-scarce scenarios for RSV. Controlled retrospective ablations allowed for additional explorations of the impact of optimization target and instruction-following on forecast accuracy. Preliminary experiments indicate that ERA’s search optimization metric influences behavior of output forecasts, and using higher-tier language models in-search improves predictive performance. By autonomously generating interpretable code that creates epidemiologically relevant predictions, this framework provides a path toward rapidly scaling high-quality disease forecasting.

## Introduction

Forecasting disease outbreaks is of critical importance for public health monitoring and response planning. In the past 15 years, the sophistication of probabilistic forecasting for epidemiology has increased dramatically in the United States (US). With some centralization of epidemiological forecasting efforts beginning prior to 202040, 15, 21, 24, the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated research and integration of forecasts into public health communication and decision-making36, 34, 27. Much of the innovation in these fields has been driven by collaborative modeling challenges run by governmental agencies or academic groups. These open challenges, many of which follow an emerging set of data standards for the field22, accept submissions from any research team, focus on transparency and careful evaluation, and typically integrate with public health decision-makers34. This allows different research groups with their own modeling expertise and opinions to contribute to a collective effort to improve disease forecasting.

The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) runs such collaborative forecasting hubs for major seasonal respiratory diseases, including influenza (FluSight7), COVID-19 (COVIDHub13), and, more recently, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV; RSVHub8). Each week, updated surveillance data are released and participating teams submit standardized probabilistic forecasts for upcoming weeks. These hubs share a common operational structure and state-level public health surveillance data source, with weekly submissions and jurisdictional targets, with the main outcome incident hospital admissions. Prior seasons have shown that models contributed by academic, governmental and industry research teams routinely outperform simple reference models such as seasonal average and persistence models, a result that has been shown consistently across infectious disease forecasting challenges in the US, United Kingdom and France 26, 33, 14, 29, 37, 27.

There is a wide diversity of different models submitted by individual teams: while some implement explicit mechanistic models of disease transmission (e.g., compartmental state-space formulations representing different stages of infection), others use methods from classical statistical frameworks (e.g., auto-regressive or spatio-temporal regression models) or machine learning (ML; e.g., random forests or neural networks). Additionally, many models hybridize these approaches, taking inspiration from a mechanistic understanding of disease transmission without explicitly building a compartmental model but rather implementing these concepts via statistical or ML techniques. Careful post-hoc evaluation has not shown consistent patterns of one kind of model outperforming others 26, 33, 14, 25. However, probabilistic ensemble forecasts that combine these individual contributed models consistently rank near the top of leaderboards 26, 35, 29, 14, 23, 25, and thus serve as state-of-the-art forecasts for public health stakeholders.

This paper examines whether Large Language Models (LLMs) in an agentic harness can create epidemiological prediction models at the same level of skill as those created by teams in the forecast hubs. If so, this could have widespread implications for epidemiological forecasting: the current methodology is labor intensive, requiring many groups to build and maintain individual operational models. Under the current system, expanding CDC-style hubs to different countries and infections is labor intensive, with the main bottleneck being the lack of humans who can code appropriate and accurate epidemiological models22, 34. Automation could make it possible to do this at a larger scale by allowing public health officials with epidemiological expertise but not expert-level programming skills to orchestrate creation of a diverse array of models for a specific predictive challenge.

We build on our previous work2, which showed that an LLM-based tree search algorithm called Empirical Research Assistance (ERA) demonstrated competitive performance on COVID-19 forecasting tasks compared to models written by experts when evaluated retrospectively. ERA uses an agentic harness based on Monte Carlo Tree Search, inspired by AlphaGo38. By framing the creation of empirical software as a ‘scorable task’ to optimize, the system iteratively generated, evaluated, and refined Python code to minimize historical forecasting error. When seeded with high-level descriptions of established epidemiological methods extracted from the literature, the search autonomously discovered and hybridized modeling strategies, ultimately generating multiple models that performed on par with or better than the official COVIDHub ensemble in retrospective analyses2. However, rigorous evaluation in time-series forecasting settings such as this requires prospective, out-of-sample forecasting. Retrospective studies inherently risk data leakage and hindsight bias regarding a pathogen’s overall trajectory, and often fail to capture the chaotic realities of live forecasting, such as data reporting delays, mid-season shifts in disease dynamics, holiday anomalies, and subsequent data revisions, sometimes called ‘backfill’14, 37, 25, 33.

For that reason, in this paper we report a fully prospective analysis of ERA-generated models during the 2025-26 forecasting season across all three CDC Forecast Hubs—FluSight7, COVIDHub13, and RSVHub8. We executed ERA tree searches seeded with 90 unique candidate model prompts, producing over 207,500 individual candidate models. From these, we selected 54 models (by validation score and method diversity) and published them in the public GoogleHub** * github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/epi_forecasts on the Google Research GitHub repository. A subset of 19 models were further designated to serve as components of a Google Research ensemble, yielding one forecast per pathogen, each submitted weekly in real time to the relevant CDC hub with auditable time stamps (Supplementary Fig. 1). Human involvement in this process comprised setup and supervision of ERA runs (S.M., M.P., Z.S.), broader guidance on the use of the system (M.P.B., B.P.W.), and epidemiological modeling expertise (N.G.R.).

Additionally, we adapted this forecasting setup for two exploratory retrospective experiments: (1) analyzing how the choice of search optimization metric influences forecast behavior, and (2) exploring different configurations of ERA, including different Gemini tiers and an in-search ‘judge,’ which can provide necessary guidance for the single-objective ERA search when strict methodological constraints are desired.

This paper demonstrates that ERA can generate, adapt, and replicate epidemiological forecasting models across a range of methodologies that, when ensembled, outperform current state-of-the-art methods and the gold-standard CDC hub ensembles—with the resulting Google-SAI ensemble officially recognized by the CDC as the top-performing model of the 2025–26 season10. This automated development strategy demonstrates the advantages of a wider and deeper iterative exploration of modeling approaches and problem design than current standard practice of manual, bespoke model development allows, while also highlighting the value of human expertise in guiding model selection and development.

## Results

We first outline our prospective results, showing model performance on each of the CDC’s forecasting competitions during the 2025–26 forecasting season, as well as model performance of the individual models submitted to GoogleHub. We then present results from two retrospective influenza forecasting ablation experiments: (1) changing the optimization metric used for evaluation during ERA model search; and (2) examining instruction-following capability of ERA under different configurations.

### Prospective Model Performance

#### Task, evaluation, and model selection.

Each week, updated surveillance data on respiratory diseases in the US are released and participating teams submit standardized probabilistic forecasts to the CDC’s FluSight7, COVIDHub13 and RSVHub8. The main target for each prediction challenge is incident hospital admissions across 53 jurisdictions (50 states, Washington DC, Puerto Rico, and the entire US)†† † While the CDC hubs accept optional submissions for the entire US, our pipeline generates and evaluates forecasts for the 52 state and territory jurisdictions, excluding the national-level aggregate (see Methods for details). at horizons of zero to three weeks ahead, with each forecast represented as a predictive distribution over 23 quantiles (Fig. 1a–c). Forecasts are evaluated against observations that are released (and occasionally revised) in future weeks, and are considered final after the end of the respiratory forecasting season. This setting is a leak-proof prospective test, as no model can access the outcomes it is predicting, and all submissions carry a publicly auditable time stamp on GitHub.

Historical surveillance data (black line) are available up to the forecast origin (vertical dashed lines). At each weekly submission point, forecasts are generated for four subsequent target weeks (horizontal arrows). b Depiction of a probabilistic forecast for one jurisdiction in a submission week. Taking the end of the observed data as the origin, the model produces a full predictive distribution via 23 quantiles for each of the four target horizons. The dotted line indicates the median trajectory. c Task dimensions and scale for each pathogen: 52 US jurisdictions, 4-week horizon, 23-quantile distributions, with weekly data updates and forecast submissions. d Sample time series of weekly hospital admissions for influenza (top), COVID-19 (middle), and RSV (bottom) for California, with non-overlapping temporal splits for validation (purple), retrospective testing (orange), and prospective evaluation (green). A non-chronological ordering was used for influenza forecast validation because the most recent season before the held-out set was deemed to be an overly challenging test set due to it being a unusually high influenza season (see Methods).*

We treated this forecasting task as an automated model discovery problem, deploying ERA to generate, evaluate, and iteratively refine code for candidate forecasting models. Given a natural language task specification, access to historical surveillance data, an evaluation harness with a defined objective function, and a computational sandbox with access to relevant scientific libraries, ERA uses an LLM-guided tree search to explore the space of possible modeling approaches autonomously (Fig. 2). At each node of the search tree, the LLM reads and modifies the previous model code, the modified model is executed and scored on a validation period, and the score is used to guide subsequent search branching decisions. To guard against overfitting to the validation period, all candidate nodes are additionally evaluated on a separate retrospective test set (Fig. 1d, Supplementary Table 1), and final models selected on the basis of combined performance across both periods (see Methods). Models were deployed prospectively starting in November 2025; real-time forecasts were submitted to the CDC hubs and pushed weekly to the GoogleHub repository for transparent evaluation over the season.

*Figure 2: The ERA System Architecture. The ERA workflow automates the translation of natural language scientific model statements into optimized executable code. Inputs: ERA ingests a natural language problem statement, datasets, and an evaluation harness. Processing: An LLM-driven tree search explores a high-dimensional solution space, generating and refining Python implementations of epidemiological models. Output: ERA returns the entire search tree, including Python code and a corresponding evaluation score for each node. ERA identifies the best-scoring solution—a mathematically optimized model that minimizes the defined loss function while adhering to architectural constraints.*

Models were scored during search using the Weighted Interval Score (WIS; equation (1) in Methods), a proper scoring rule well-matched to the 23-quantile submission format, and one that approximates the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS), a well-known probabilistic evaluation metric 6. All leaderboard comparisons reported in this paper use WIS applied to log-transformed targets and quantiles (referred to throughout as ‘log WIS’), a choice recommended for epidemiological forecast evaluation4 and consistent with the official CDC hub evaluation framework.

To promote architectural diversity, we supplied ERA with a structured set of diverse prompts containing instructions drawn from the metadata of other CDC-submitting models, relevant epidemiological modeling literature, and suggestions from Gemini Deep Research (Methods).

Around the beginning of the prospective submissions for each pathogen, we selected 34 influenza models, 18 COVID-19 models, and two RSV models from the full pool of generated candidates on the basis of retrospective validation and test performance (see Equation (3) and Supplementary Section G for test and validation scores for all models), with an additional emphasis on maintaining methodological diversity across the selected set. The significantly smaller RSV model pool reflects the pathogen’s recent addition to forecast hubs and the limited number of available seasons of historical target data. We submitted predictions from these models weekly with time stamps to GoogleHub. From these, we selected a subset of models (seven for influenza, ten for COVID-19 and two for RSV), for inclusion in the three Google-SAI submissions–the ensemble models submitted by Google Research’s Science AI team to the CDC forecasting hubs. Ensembles are calculated by a direct quantile average of component forecasts (Methods). Figure 3a shows example forecasts for California for each of the three Google-SAI ensemble models.

#### Ensembles of ERA-generated models perform competitively across pathogens.

Google-SAI ensembles achieved top-tier performance across all three pathogens for the 2025-26 forecasting season. Figure 3b shows the Google-SAI ensembles achieving the best pairwise relative log WIS across all CDC hub-submitted models. Supplementary Tables 2, 4, 6 provide a complete summary of performance of all models analyzed in this paper, including absolute and pairwise relative WIS and log WIS, mean absolute error (MAE), and coverage of 95% prediction intervals; the Google-SAI ensembles display competitive performance across all four metrics and has the best on pairwise relative log-scale WIS, the official metric used to rank models by CDC10. We start our analysis period from the first valid submission of the Google-SAI ensemble to each CDC hub (see Supplementary Sections 1, 2, 3). The task space for all analyses covers 52 jurisdictions (50 states, plus Washington DC and Puerto Rico) and four horizons (Fig. 1c). For influenza, we evaluate models on a task space including 28 reference dates. Eligible models were those submitting predictions for $\geq 80\%$ of tasks ( $\geq 4,659$ tasks). Google_SAI-FluEns ranked first among 43 eligible submissions (out of 57 total models submitting at least one prediction to FluSight) by pairwise relative season-average mean log WIS, with a score of 0.91 vs. 1.0 for the official FluSight-ensemble, which is created by taking the median across all eligible team submissions to the hub. Google_SAI-FluEnsalso ranks first in the CDC’s official FluSight evaluation of the 2025-26 season10. For COVID-19, we consider 25 reference dates with the same task space coverage as for influenza, resulting in a minimum required task space of $4,160$ tasks. Google_SAI-Ensemble ranked first across 11 eligible COVIDHub submissions (out of 17 total), also outperforming CovidHub-ensemble with a relative log WIS of 0.96. RSV models are evaluated over 23 reference dates, with the same eligibility criteria, i.e., models must have scorable predictions for $\geq 3,660$ tasks. Google_SAI-RSVEns ranked first among the four eligible RSVHub submissions (out of nine total), outperforming RSVHub-ensemble with a relative log WIS of 0.89.

Jurisdiction-level forecast plots for all three pathogens (Supplementary Figs. 2, 6, 10) illustrate the behavior of these ensemble forecasts and of the ground truth observations across the analyzed reference dates. Nearly all locations saw a clear ‘seasonal peak’ for influenza during the forecasting period. For COVID and RSV, the magnitude of a seasonal rise and fall varied by location. For influenza, the ensemble median roughly tracked the observed seasonal trajectory, although it tended to under-predict as the season initially progressed and over-predict after the season peak. Predictive intervals were wider during the rapid epidemic ascent in December 2025 and tightened through the peak and decline phases from January 2026 onward. COVID-19 forecasts were generated over a more gradual seasonal peak in most locations. RSV exhibited the most heterogeneous state-level dynamics, with greater variation in the timing and shape of epidemic curves, and correspondingly wider predictive intervals throughout the season. Overall, wider prediction intervals indicate greater uncertainty about future epidemic trajectories, while narrower intervals indicate greater confidence in the range of likely outcomes. Additionally, Supplementary Figs. 3, 7, and 11 show each of the Google-SAI models achieving clearly better-than-average performance across all jurisdictions as compared to other models submitting to the CDC hubs, with the exception only of Hawaii for COVID-19.

This pattern of competitive consistency is preserved across all prediction horizons from zero to three weeks ahead (Supplementary Tables 3, 5, and 7). For all three pathogens the Google-SAI ensembles track within the top cluster of submitted models by log WIS at every horizon, well below the CDC baselines, and maintain their relative positions without degradation at longer lead times.

WIS is the sum of three components describing forecast behavior: dispersion (width of the predicted distribution), overprediction, and underprediction 5. We plot the decomposed season average WIS for the top-performing eligible models submitting to each CDC forecasting hub in Supplementary Figs. 4, 8, 12. Across pathogens, Google-SAI models exhibited a consistent asymmetry in their WIS decomposition, with underprediction contributing more to mean WIS than overprediction. This asymmetry was relatively weak for COVID-19, more apparent for influenza, and strongest for RSV, where underprediction accounted for nearly 60% of the total score. This trend of insufficient coverage of unexpectedly high incidence appears across models for all three pathogens, potentially indicating a fundamental challenge in the prediction of the onset and exponential growth of outbreaks.

Standardized ranks provide an additional task-level view of relative performance, showing whether a model is consistently competitive across forecasts or performs well on average despite occasional poor rankings. For each task, a standardized rank of one indicates the best log WIS among submitting models, while a rank of zero indicates the worst (see Methods for details). The standardized log WIS rank distribution of FluSight-submitting models (Supplementary Fig. 5) shows substantial variability in individual model performance. Among eligible models, excluding FluSight-ensemble, Google_SAI-FluEns had the highest first quartile rank, meaning it ranked near the bottom less often than any other individual model. Some models achieved high ranks more frequently, but also had more frequent low-ranking forecasts. Consistent with previous findings14, FluSight-ensemble had a narrower standardized rank distribution than most individual models, indicating that it was rarely either the best or worst performer. This is expected for an ensemble that combines multiple component models, as ensembles tend to be more robust across forecasting conditions rather than dominant on every individual task. While Google_SAI-FluEns is also an ensemble, its component models are fewer in number (seven versus 43), which limits the diversity-driven stabilization that characterizes hub ensembles with many independent contributors. The standardized rank distributions for the Google-SAI ensembles for COVID-19 (Supplementary Fig. 9) and RSV (Supplementary Fig. 13) show similar patterns. Google_SAI-Ensemble ranked second among COVIDHub submissions, and Google_SAI-RSVEns ranked first among RSVHub submissions with the smallest first quartile of standardized ranks.

#### Discovery of diverse forecasting architectures.

All Google-SAI component models, along with additional candidate models, were submitted as individual forecasts to GoogleHub throughout the prospective season. These models were generated using a structured set of prompts containing summarized method instructions from three broad categories: (1) scientist-inspired methods adapted from existing literature and documentation on human-developed models, (2) recombinations that combine pairs of distinct methodological frameworks, and (3) AI-led methods, where an LLM suggests the modeling approach rather than following a human-specified methodology (see Methods for additional detail). Figure 4 shows the relative log WIS of every model in this repository against the respective CDC hub ensemble (values below one indicate better-than-CDC-ensemble performance), alongside several top-performing independently submitted models from each hub for context.

Across all three hubs, Google-SAI ensemble forecasts achieved the best relative log WIS scores across all internal component models and all top-performing hub-submitting models (Fig. 4). For influenza, two ERA-generated component models from our prospective time-stamped repository additionally outperformed FluSight-ensemble. Of these, one is an adaptation of an existing ‘scientist-inspired’ method (G-Cornell_JHU-hierarchSIR), and the other a ‘recombination’, a hybrid of LANL-DBM and LANL-Inferno. Both were included as components in Google_SAI-FluEns. For COVID-19, two individual component models also outperformed CovidHub-ensemble: a scientist-inspired adaptation (G-CADPH-CovidCAT_Ensemble) and a recombination (CMU_TimeSeries and UMASS_gbqr). Similarly, for RSV, both individual AI-led models out-performed RSVHub-Ensemble.

Pairwise comparisons between ERA-generated adaptations and their human-authored reference models reveal that ERA-generated models can either ameliorate or degrade performance as compared to their original scientist-created counterparts. No single prompting strategy reliably yields only good models (Fig. 4). Prompts grounded in established domain literature (scientist-inspired) and those ‘recombining’ different paradigms can provide models that forecast competitively in mature contexts such as influenza and COVID-19, but equally produce poorer-performing models. Methodological diversity is a well-established driver of ensemble forecast skill 14. Our results suggest this principle extends to automated model generation: aggregating models across all three prompt strategies yields ensemble predictions that consistently outperform both individual components and CDC hub ensembles.

However, the above comment on diversity applies to the methodologies requested in the scientist-inspired prompts, rather than necessarily those implemented by the generated models. To assess methodological fidelity, a subject-matter expert reviewed the 24 scientist-inspired ERA-generated influenza models submitted to GoogleHub in the prospective study and classified each according to how faithfully it implemented the requested methodology (Supplementary Table 2; see Methods). Of the 24 models, 17 successfully followed the instructions, four implemented the requested methodology only partially, and three failed to implement it. Partial or failed implementations were concentrated among prompts specifying more complex mechanistic or statistical approaches, with omitted or approximated components including Kalman filtering and explicit compartmental models, and some models instead implementing simpler ML approaches such as gradient boosting. We investigate this limitation further in a subsequent exploratory analysis. Importantly, the expert assessments for the component models selected for Google_SAI-FluEns (Supplementary Table 2) confirm that, despite occasional instruction-following failures, the final ensemble retains methodological diversity across mechanistic, statistical, and machine learning paradigms.

### Retrospective Experiments

#### Internal optimization metrics shape forecast behavior.

Beyond generating performant, production-ready models to predict outbreaks, the ERA pipeline provides a systematic experimental mechanism to explore how problem framing impacts forecast behavior. To explore the effects of ERA optimization metric on model output, we evaluated three candidate metrics drawn from the two principal families of proper scoring rules for probabilistic forecasting 18. The first is CRPS, which measures the integrated squared difference between the predictive cumulative distribution function (CDF) and the empirical CDF of the observation. The WIS used in analyses in the previous section is a quantile-based approximation of CRPS 6. The second is the Logarithmic Score (Log Score), a classical proper scoring rule based on the log-probability assigned to the observed outcome; to frame this as an optimization loss, we evaluate the negative log-probability, where a lower score indicates better performance. The third is Log-scale CRPS, a CRPS variant in which both predictions and observations are log-transformed prior to scoring (as for log WIS), combining the distributional breadth of CRPS with greater sensitivity to relative errors at low counts. See Methods (Equations (4)–(6)) for more detailed explanations of these scoring functions.

We used ERA to search for influenza models with the same data splits as described in Fig. 1, but varied the optimization metric used for in-search evaluation. For each metric, we ran five independent replicas of 2,500-node searches. Supplementary Figure 14 shows how the search evolved under each metric by tracking the cumulative best score—the in-search validation score of the best model found so far at each point in the search. These curves reveal differences across metrics in both search efficiency and out-of-sample generalization. The continuous gradients provided by distance-based metrics (CRPS and Log CRPS) allow the search to identify performant architectures rapidly, with cumulative best test scores generally reaching their minimum between 500 and 750 nodes (Supplementary Fig. 14, left and middle columns). However, searches under these metrics are also clearly susceptible to overfitting, visible in later stages of the search as rising test curves (orange) concurrent with falling validation curves (purple). Because of this late-stage overfitting, the final validation-selected models optimized for one metric do not always achieve the best test performance on that metric: notably, optimizing for standard CRPS yields better late-search test performance on Log CRPS (panel d) than optimizing for Log CRPS directly (panel e). Because WIS and log WIS approximate CRPS and Log CRPS, respectively, this result partially explains our strong log WIS performance in the previous section, even though those searches used WIS as the optimization metric. This late-stage overfitting also reinforces the need to select best ERA nodes by selection score (see Methods, Equation (3)), which includes components for both validation and test scores (with a larger weighting on test score), rather than directly by validation score.

We therefore selected a single best node from each replica using this score and evaluated its test-period forecasts across all three metrics. Fig. 5 illustrates the resulting test-period forecasts from the best node of one replica for each metric in three selected states‡‡ ‡ The selected states are broadly representative of overall observed trends. Although all three models slightly lag the true epidemic curve, underpredicting during the growth phase and overpredicting during the decline, the size of these errors and the shape of the predictive distributions differ qualitatively by metric. The CRPS-optimized model tracks the observed curve most closely—its medians come nearest to the observed peaks, particularly in New York, though it briefly overshoots immediately after the peak in California and Texas—and its prediction intervals contract tightly once admissions return to low levels. In contrast, the Log CRPS- and Log Score-optimized models substantially underpredict the peak in all three states. The Log Score-optimized model is further distinguished by intervals that remain wider relative to observed admissions throughout the low-incidence end of the season (March–June) in all three states, whereas CRPS intervals (and Log CRPS intervals in California and New York) collapse onto the observations. These differences are consistent with how the metrics weight errors: standard CRPS penalizes absolute errors and therefore rewards accurately capturing the high-count surge, whereas Log CRPS penalizes multiplicative (relative) errors, so underpredicting the peak by a given factor costs roughly the same as a comparable relative error at low counts. Finally, the Log Score has a very harsh penalty ( $-\infty$ ) when a model assigns no probability to the eventual outcome, so this incentivizes a wide spreading out of probability across a large range of possible outcomes.
