Forecasts are from the best node (by selection score, Equation (3)) of the first of five replicas of ERA searches optimized for CRPS (left), Log CRPS (middle), or Log Score (right). Black lines and points show observed admissions. Each connected blue line is the median forecast issued on a single reference date across its forecast horizons, and darker and lighter shading show the corresponding 50% and 95% prediction intervals (PIs); shading overlaps across consecutive forecasts.*

Supplementary Table 8 summarizes test-period forecast quality and behavior across all replicas and jurisdictions. Because post-search selection via Equation (3) avoids the late-stage overfitting seen in Supplementary Fig. 14, the selected models for each optimization metric achieve, on average, the best (lowest) test score on that metric. We additionally report mean bias (the average difference between predicted median and observed admissions), the proportions of median under- and overprediction, and the mean width of the 50% prediction interval. The two distance-based metrics (CRPS and Log CRPS) yield similar aggregate bias and interval widths. Standard CRPS achieves the smallest mean bias, most balanced under- and overprediction, and narrowest 50% prediction intervals (bolded values). Models optimized for Log Score diverge most sharply, exhibiting the strongest underprediction bias, widest prediction intervals, and highest variance across replicas. This is because Log Score assigns an effectively infinite penalty when the observed value falls outside the predicted distribution, which favors dispersed forecasts.

Together, these results show that the choice of optimization metric in ERA measurably shapes the behavior of final forecasts, and that ERA makes it practical to systematically experiment with objective functions and problem design at scale. In our exploratory analysis, standard CRPS provided the most stable search dynamics and the best-performing forecasts overall.

#### Instruction-following fidelity varies across methods and search configurations.

In the prospective evaluation, most ERA-generated models implemented the requested methodology successfully, but unsuccessful or partially successful implementations tended to substitute standard ML regressors for more specialized statistical or mechanistic approaches. This limitation is important because the strength of collaborative forecasting ensembles depends partly on methodological diversity across mechanistic, time-series, statistical, and ML models 14, 26. Reproducing that diversity with an automated system therefore requires not only instruction guidance but also a mechanism to enforce method compliance. We therefore investigated how instruction-following fidelity varied with the requested methodology and with underlying LLM, and whether fidelity could be improved by evaluating methodological compliance during the search.

We compared four ERA configurations: Gemini 2.5 Flash with an in-loop judge, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 3 Flash, and Gemini 3 Pro without a judge. We applied each configuration to four established FluSight-submitting methods representing distinct modeling strategies: UMass-gbqr32, UGA_flucast-INFLAenza16, Cornell_JHU-hierarchSIR1, and NU-PGF_FLUH39. Each configuration–method combination was evaluated in three independent runs. An external post-hoc judge, using method-specific rubrics calibrated against expert epidemiologist assessments, classified each final implementation as a ‘Match’, ‘Partial Match’, or ‘No Match’. Predictive performance was assessed using the selection score (3), with lower values indicating better forecasts (Methods).

Instruction-following fidelity varied markedly across the requested methods (Supplementary Table 9). While ten of 12 UMass-gbqr runs achieved a full match, none of the 12 NU-PGF_FLUH runs did, indicating that fidelity depended strongly on the methodology being reproduced. Higher-tier Gemini models yielded selected models with lower mean selection score for all four methods: averaging the method-level means equally, selection score decreased from 255.7 with Gemini 2.5 Flash to 164.0 with Gemini 3 Flash and 143.4 with Gemini 3 Pro. Improvements in predictive performance did not, however, consistently correspond to greater fidelity. For example, Gemini 3 Pro achieved full matches in all three Cornell_JHU-hierarchSIR runs but only partial matches in all three UGA_flucast-INFLAenza runs. The effect of the in-loop judge was similarly method dependent. Adding an in-loop judge to Gemini 2.5 Flash increased the total number of full matches from four of 12 to seven of 12 and lowered mean selection score for three of the four methods. The clearest improvement occurred for UGA_flucast-INFLAenza, for which full matches increased from one of three runs to three of three and mean selection score decreased from 316.16 to 196.51. Conversely, for Cornell_JHU-hierarchSIR, the ERA search with an in-loop judge produced one full match but increased mean selection score from 179.09 to 411.97.

Together, these results show that higher-tier LLMs consistently improved predictive performance, whereas instruction fidelity and the benefits of in-loop judging varied across methodologies. Because we evaluated only one implementation of the in-loop judge, these results do not establish whether alternative judge designs or calibration strategies would produce more consistent improvements. Full run-level results are reported in Supplementary Tables 10 for the in-loop judge and 11 for Gemini tier.

## Discussion

This work demonstrates that an LLM-guided tree search system can generate epidemiological forecasting models that compete with the state of the art across three respiratory pathogens in a fully prospective, leak-proof evaluation setting. The key finding is not that any single ERA-generated model outperforms all alternatives, but rather that the system can rapidly produce a large, methodologically diverse pool of competitive models whose ensemble matches or exceeds the gold-standard CDC hub ensembles—themselves aggregations of forecasts from dozens of expert teams 26, 35, 14. Crucially, every model in this pool is a complete, executable Python program whose forecasting logic and timestamped outputs can be read, audited, and modified by any domain scientist. Model source code and weekly forecast submissions are publicly available under the Apache 2.0 open-source license§§ § https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/epi_forecasts—a property that distinguishes ERA from black-box AutoML20 systems and aligns with the transparency increasingly emphasized in public health forecasting.

The practical implications of this automation extend beyond the specific pathogens studied here. Currently, collaborative forecasting hubs rely on sustained, labor-intensive participation of expert teams running and maintaining bespoke models week after week. This manual paradigm scales poorly to highly granular geographic resolutions (e.g., US counties), new geographic regions, or novel pathogens 40, 22. By automating model ideation, implementation, and evaluation, systems like ERA can democratize access to expert-level forecasting, providing a concrete blueprint for deploying ensemble-grade capacity at larger scales. Additionally, ERA could substantially lower the barrier to entry for hub participation, enabling rapid deployment of competitive forecasting capacity in settings that currently lack the specialized modeling workforce required. This potentially allows expanding the forecast ‘hub’ concept22 to jurisdictions and granularities where it is harder to attract expert attention.

Notably, the RSV results presented here provide a direct test of a ‘cold start’ scenario. With minimal historical data, no mature modeling literature to draw from, and a hub in its first season, ERA’s best-performing models came from unconstrained architectural searches in which the system discovered effective approaches without domain-specific guidance. While the resulting models were necessarily simpler than those generated for influenza (both were gradient-boosted pipelines fed with cross-pathogen auxiliary inputs), their top-ranked performance among the other RSVHub submissions, ensemble and baseline models demonstrates that automated search can provide useful forecasting capacity even in data-scarce regimes.

One limitation of the ERA-generated forecasts presented and evaluated in this work is that, while they achieve high accuracy scores relative to existing models, they suffer from similar systematic biases observed in other models across multiple seasons of these forecasting efforts. Forecasts of seasonal influenza and COVID-19 have struggled to capture dynamics of rapid increase and decrease during seasonal epidemics: models tend to underestimate the rate of increase as the epidemic is rising and the rate of decrease as it falls23, 14, 25. Forecasts generated by ERA are no exception. However, this reflects not so much a limitation of the ERA model generation pipeline as it does a structural challenge with developing a set of scorable tasks for epidemic forecasting that incentivize forecasts which can be used for improving situational awareness during seasonal outbreaks or for decision-support. Developing evaluation rubrics that are aligned with public health decision-making is an active area of research3, 17, 28, and systems like ERA highlight possibilities for training models that have been optimized for specific contexts. Indeed, our retrospective comparison of optimization metrics serves as a first step in this direction. By demonstrating that the ERA search is responsive to the mathematical properties of its reward signal, we highlight how forecasters can use this pipeline to rapidly discover novel architectures tailored to specific settings or requirements.

A second limitation concerns the ensemble aggregation strategy itself. In this study, the submitted ensemble forecast was computed as a simple, equally weighted median across component models—an approach that, while robust and well-established in forecasting practice 35, makes no attempt to learn from the relative strengths and weaknesses of its components. Yet the forecasting task is inherently high-dimensional: individual models may excel in different jurisdictions, at different forecast horizons, or under different epidemic conditions such as rapid growth versus post-peak decline. The optimal combination strategy is therefore not a single set of static weights but a context-dependent mapping—itself a challenging optimization problem 12, 31. Framing ensemble construction as a scorable task and applying ERA’s tree search to find effective adaptive weighting schemes or selection logic is a natural direction for future work.

A further limitation of the prospective evaluation is that not all models are assessed on identical sets of forecasting tasks. Models join hubs at different points in the season, occasionally skip submission weeks, or cover different subsets of jurisdictions, meaning that each pairwise comparison is computed over a different intersection of shared tasks. While the pairwise relative scoring framework we adopt (following established practice 6) mitigates this by computing score ratios only over mutually completed tasks and then averaging across all opponents, it does not fully eliminate the issue: a model that begins submitting after a particularly difficult or easy phase of the epidemic is effectively evaluated on a different forecasting problem than one that was active throughout. We partially address this by imposing an 80% task-coverage eligibility threshold, but acknowledge that strict like-for-like comparison across all models remains infeasible in any real-time collaborative forecasting setting. The prospective evaluation is also restricted to subnational forecasts: we did not generate or submit forecasts for the national US target accepted by the CDC Hubs, and all evaluations therefore concern state- and territory-level jurisdictions.

While traditional algorithms are expected to be deterministic from end to end, ERA automates the exploratory model search process typically performed by human scientists, a process that is itself inherently non-reproducible. Because ERA operates as a stochastic search algorithm subject to multiple sources of randomness, independent searches seeded with the same prompt will naturally yield distinct outputs. This variability is compounded by the rapid development cycle of foundation models; for instance, the majority of the models composing the Google-SAI ensembles were generated using Gemini 2.5 Flash, a model scheduled for deprecation in October 202619. However, this stochasticity in the discovery phase does not compromise the reproducibility of our results. The ERA-produced model codes (and their corresponding forecasts) used in this study are entirely deterministic, auditable, and reproducible. Rather than guaranteeing identical code generation across different search runs, ERA’s contribution lies in discovering transparent, executable Python code that scientists can reliably run, inspect, and maintain to reproduce the forecasts and analysis reported here.

More broadly, the computational footprint of our prospective campaign—142 tree searches of up to 2,500 nodes each—should be viewed as a snapshot of foundation model capabilities in the Fall of 2025, when candidate code had to be frozen prior to the start of the forecasting season. ERA’s extensive tree search over thousands of nodes was originally designed to compensate for the higher coding and reasoning error rates of earlier-generation LLMs. As shown in our retrospective comparisons across Gemini tiers, newer frontier models generate performant, compliant forecasting code in substantially fewer attempts; consequently, research teams deploying agentic forecasting pipelines today would likely require far smaller search budgets than the 2,500-node limit used here.

The retrospective experiments presented in Results reveal the capabilities and structural limitations of the current system. The bias toward gradient-boosted implementations—observed even when the search was explicitly prompted with mechanistic or statistical instructions—likely reflects a fundamental asymmetry in the training distribution across the Google Gemini model tiers tested in this study: standard software patterns are more reliably generated than highly specialized scientific frameworks. We showed that two complementary interventions can partially mitigate this bias: using more capable foundation models (Gemini 3 Pro achieved full fidelity on some of the more complex methods where Gemini Flash models could not), and deploying an LLM judge-in-the-loop to gate non-compliant implementations. However, for the most specialized methods (e.g., NU-PGF_FLUH) neither intervention was sufficient to achieve full methodological fidelity. We emphasize that these instruction-following and in-loop judge experiments were designed as small-scale exploratory analyses rather than an exhaustive benchmark, and could not be expanded further on the prospective baseline model due to the scheduled deprecation of Gemini 2.5 Flash

Our results suggest that expert human judgment still plays a meaningful role in guiding model development, even in a highly automated forecasting pipeline like ERA. The Google team that drove this project included several scientists, analysts, and engineers (without explicit infectious disease or epidemiological training) and one expert consultant from academia who has participated in epidemiological forecasting challenges for over ten years. While the tree search experiments were orchestrated, compiled and analyzed by the Google engineers, the expert provided input on ERA prompt framing and which existing models to prioritize exploring, and gave judgments on how faithful the ERA-generated re-implementations of models were. Additionally, the epidemiology expert identified and suggested two models that were highly performant on FluSight Forecast Hub several years ago but were no longer currently submitting: LANL-DBM and LANL-Inferno. ERA implemented a recombination of these models, and this adaptation was one of the top-scoring models from GoogleHub (Figure 4). Our Google-SAI ensembles were also generated using a direct average of human-selected models from the ERA-generated pool. Although we could have automated model selection using validation and retrospective test scores, this would not have considered model diversity. Therefore, we suggest there is some anecdotal evidence that even in the presence of a highly automated LLM-driven model-generation architecture, there remains a place for human expertise to highlight and drive opportunities for model exploration.

Our prospective results demonstrate that autonomous LLM-guided tree search can operate reliably under the rigors of real-time public health surveillance, producing transparent, auditable forecasting software that outperforms state-of-the-art human-curated ensembles across multiple pathogens. Rather than replacing domain scientists with black-box predictions, systems like ERA shift the role of human expertise from labor-intensive software implementation to high-level scientific direction, including defining epidemiological hypotheses, curating data, and designing evaluation rubrics that align with public health needs. By dramatically lowering the engineering barrier required to create and maintain diverse model ensembles, autonomous code discovery offers a scalable blueprint for rapid outbreak response across new pathogens, granular geographies, and resource-limited public health settings.

## Methods

### 1 Data and Forecasting Task

This study focuses on forecasting hospital admissions resulting from three major seasonal respiratory pathogens in the US: influenza, COVID-19, and RSV. Unlike retrospective ‘hindcasting,’ this work implemented a real-time prospective study, requiring models to generate predictions before the ground-truth observations were recorded. This approach subjects the forecasting process to real-time surveillance conditions, including reporting delays and data revisions typical of live national healthcare systems.

The scale of the forecasting task is high-dimensional, requiring full geographic coverage of the US. Models provide predictions for 52 jurisdictions, including all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico. Although the CDC hubs also accept optional submissions for the national-level US aggregate (a 53rd jurisdiction), we excluded the national target from our pipeline: national admission counts are an order of magnitude larger than individual state counts (which can disproportionately dominate training loss if pooled), and predictive quantiles cannot be directly summed across states without explicitly modeling cross-jurisdiction covariance. Because the CDC evaluates state-level performance separately from national-level forecasts using pairwise comparisons over shared tasks, omitting the national aggregate does not incur any penalty in hub evaluations. For each jurisdiction, forecasts must cover the four time horizons required by the CDC Forecast Hubs, from zero to three weeks ahead (Fig. 1c). Additionally, to characterize the uncertainty of future disease trajectories, forecasts are produced in a probabilistic format rather than as single-point estimates. As illustrated in Fig. 1b, for each target week, models generate a predictive distribution represented by 23 specific quantiles (ranging from 0.01 to 0.99). This allows submissions to represent the full range of potential outcomes, from the expected median trajectory to the low-probability tails of the distribution that represent extreme surge events. Together, these requirements result in the generation of 4,784 unique prediction points per infection type (calculated as 52 jurisdictions $\times$ 4 horizons $\times$ 23 quantiles) every week.

The primary data source for inputs and targets was the CDC’s Weekly Hospital Respiratory Data (HRD) from the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) 9. As shown in Fig. 1a, the study follows a rolling-origin submission scheme where new data are released weekly, encouraging a corresponding weekly forecast submission. During our study period, this resulted in a total of 28 weekly submissions for influenza, 25 for COVID-19, and 24 for RSV, of which 23 were included in the analysis (the first submission was excluded due to an operational error in the submission pipeline).

In our pipeline, preprocessing consisted of extracting jurisdiction-level weekly admission counts, cleaning non-numeric entries, and linearly interpolating any missing weeks to produce a complete time series grid across all 52 jurisdictions. The specific input features available to each pathogen’s ERA setup differed based on data availability and relevance. Following the practice of other successful forecasting models32, ERA-generated influenza models received weekly incident influenza hospitalizations and were supplemented with a longer history of outpatient syndromic surveillance data from the CDC’s ILINet system11(which predates the current target series by more than two decades, offering a longer record of seasonal trends for influenza-like illnesses). COVID-19 models received weekly incident COVID-19 hospitalizations. RSV models received weekly hospitalizations for all three pathogens along with ILINet data to supplement the short history of the target (see Methods 5.1). Beyond this standardized preprocessing, each generated model was free to implement its own additional feature engineering within the ERA sandbox.

The temporal data for each pathogen were divided into three non-overlapping splits to ensure rigorous evaluation: Validation, Retrospective Test, and Prospective Held-out (Fig. 1d, Supplementary Table 1). The Validation block was used during search for optimization; the Retrospective Test block was used post-search for node selection (Methods 4.2); and the Prospective Held-out period represents the live evaluation phase, where model performance was recorded in real-time against data that did not exist during the development phase. For influenza, we chose to not use the most recent season as the Retrospective Test season and instead use the 2022/2023 season. This was because the 2024/2025 season was in many locations unusually high, and we thought that it might penalize model formulations too harshly in the test phase.

The above procedure was applied for the prospective and retrospective studies reported in Results. While our prospective forecasts were generated in real-time using preliminary, less complete data snapshots and evaluated using the finalized data, the retrospective analyses used the updated (revised and back-filled) versions of the data. However, we note that this distinction is not a threat to the study’s validity because retrospective models are compared solely against each other in internal benchmarks rather than being measured against historical real-time hub submissions.

### 2 Evaluation Metrics

This study evaluates forecasts using variants of the Weighted Interval Score (WIS). WIS is a proper scoring rule that penalizes both lack of precision (wide intervals) and poor calibration (ground truth falling outside the predicted quantiles). Small WIS values imply predictions are both sharp and well-calibrated.

Formally, let $F$ denote a predictive distribution of the quantity of interest $Y$ with median $m$ and central prediction intervals at levels $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{K}$ , where $l_{\alpha_{k}}$ and $u_{\alpha_{k}}$ are the $\alpha_{k}/2$ and $1-\alpha_{k}/2$ quantiles of $F$ . The WIS for an observed value $y$ is defined as 6

$$ \text{WIS}(F,y)=\frac{1}{K+0.5}\left(w_{0}\,|y-m|\;+\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\cdot\text{IS}_{\alpha_{k}}(F,y)\right), $$

where $w_{0}=0.5$ , $w_{k}=\alpha_{k}/2$ , and the interval score for level $\alpha_{k}$ is

$$ \text{IS}_{\alpha_{k}}(F,y)=(u_{\alpha_{k}}-l_{\alpha_{k}})+\frac{2}{\alpha_{k}}(l_{\alpha_{k}}-y)\,\mathbb{1}(y<l_{\alpha_{k}})+\frac{2}{\alpha_{k}}(y-u_{\alpha_{k}})\,\mathbb{1}(y>u_{\alpha_{k}}). $$

In this study, forecasts are represented by 23 quantiles corresponding to $K=11$ central prediction intervals plus the median, yielding $\alpha_{k}\in\{0.02,0.05,\ldots,0.80,0.90\}$ .

The log WIS variant used for official CDC leaderboard rankings applies the same WIS formula (1) to log-transformed predictions and observations, i.e., inputs are transformed following $\tilde{y}=\log(1+y)$ , where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and the offset of one accommodates possible zero counts. Concretely, let $\tilde{F}$ denote the predictive distribution of $\log(1+Y)$ induced by $F$ , or, equivalently, the distribution with quantiles $\log(1+l_{\alpha_{k}}),\log(1+u_{\alpha_{k}})$ , and median $\log(1+m)$ . Then, $\text{log\,WIS}=\text{WIS}(\tilde{F},\tilde{y})$ .

Because not all models submit predictions for the same set of tasks—some join later in the season, omit certain reference dates, or cover fewer jurisdictions or prediction horizons—direct comparison of mean absolute scores can be misleading. We therefore report pairwise relative WIS 14 as the primary model comparison metric in aggregated settings. For each pair of models $(i,j)$ , the ratio of their mean scores is computed over the intersection of tasks both models submitted; the relative score for model $i$ is then the geometric mean of these pairwise ratios across all opponents $j\neq i$ . We rescale scores so the relevant CDC hub ensemble reports a score of one, and scores below this indicate better-than-ensemble performance. We compute this metric for WIS and log WIS, and report both in Supplementary Tables 2, 4, and 6. Pairwise relative log WIS serves as the primary ranking metric throughout the prospective comparisons in this work, as it does in official CDC comparisons10.

As seen in Equation (2), the interval score strictly partitions into three distinct penalty components: dispersion $(u_{\alpha_{k}}-l_{\alpha_{k}})$ , which measures the inherent width or uncertainty of the forecast; overprediction $\frac{2}{\alpha_{k}}(l_{\alpha_{k}}-y)\,\mathbf{1}(y<l_{\alpha_{k}})$ , which penalizes the model when the true observation falls below the predicted interval; and underprediction $\frac{2}{\alpha_{k}}(y-u_{\alpha_{k}})\,\mathbf{1}(y>u_{\alpha_{k}})$ , which applies when the observation falls above it. By summing these components separately across all $K$ intervals via Equation (1), we can distinguish models that are uninformative because of excessive hedging (dominated by dispersion) from those suffering from severe directional biases (dominated by over- or underprediction) that a single aggregate score would obscure. We plot WIS decomposition in Supplementary Figs. 4, 8, 12.

Additionally, to complement these aggregate scores with a measure of consistency, we report standardized ranks 14. For each individual forecasting task (a unique combination of jurisdiction, horizon, and reference date), all submitting models are ranked by log WIS and the ranks linearly rescaled to $[0,1]$ , where $1$ denotes the best-performing model on that task and $0$ the worst. The resulting distribution of standardized ranks across tasks summarizes how frequently a model performs near the top or bottom of the model set, capturing variability in performance that aggregate mean scores alone would obscure.

An additional qualitative evaluation assessed whether the ERA-generated code followed the methodological instructions provided in each prompt (Supplementary Table 2). One coauthor (N.G.R.) reviewed the instruction text and corresponding output code and classified each model as ‘Success’, ‘Partial fail’, or ‘Fail’. Models classified as Success’ followed all instructions that were feasible within the connected sandbox, excluding requests to access unavailable data or libraries. ‘Partial fail’ indicated that most major components were implemented but one or more substantive methodological requirements were omitted or approximated (for example, omitting a requested Kalman filter or implementing an approximation rather than an explicit compartmental model). ‘Fail’ indicated that the requested methodology was largely or entirely disregarded (for example, implementing gradient boosting when an SIR-type model was requested).

### 3 The ERA Framework

Empirical Research Assistance (ERA) is an autonomous system that automates development of empirical software for scorable scientific tasks2. It searches over the space of code implementations using a tree search algorithm: each node in the tree corresponds to a concrete implementation of the required task, including specific combinations of feature engineering, data preprocessing, and model architecture, and is scored against a predefined objective function. Node selection for tree expansion balances exploitation of the highest-scoring candidates with exploration of less-visited ones via a Predictor + Upper Confidence bound applied to Trees (PUCT) algorithm.

The search is guided by an LLM—specifically, by one of the Gemini family of models—acting as an agent that generates, tests, and refines Python code. Starting from a natural language problem statement, the agent proposes initial architectures and iteratively improves them based on execution feedback and performance scores (Fig. 2). This branching structure allows the system to explore multiple modeling paradigms simultaneously (executing on ten parallel threads), learning from the successes and failures of previous nodes to discover increasingly effective solutions. To manage computational resources and ensure system stability, ERA search trajectories are bounded by dual constraints: a maximum number of explored nodes and a cumulative execution time limit within the sandbox environment.

To maintain scientific rigor and prevent data leakage, ERA operates within a secure, immutable evaluation harness. This harness contains relevant ground truth datasets and evaluation logic but is entirely hidden from the LLM agent. The agent can submit code to the harness and receive performance metrics and error logs, but it cannot modify the evaluation protocol or access ground-truth data from the held-out periods. This ‘blind’ evaluation ensures discovered models are robust and prevents the system from ‘hacking’ evaluation criteria.

### 4 ERA Configuration for Epidemiological Forecasting

This section describes two task-specific design choices made to apply ERA to multi-pathogen forecasting: a structured prompting strategy across multiple search modes, and a two-stage model selection scheme that separates search-time scoring from post-search node selection. Both are part of the pipeline used to generate models for prospective submission to the CDC hubs.

#### 4.1 Method Prompt Sources

Each independent ERA search used for this analysis ran for up to $2,500$ generated nodes or until a cumulative sandbox execution time limit of $2500$ hours over ten parallel threads was reached, whichever came first. Because candidate evaluations within each search tree were executed across ten parallel sandbox threads, the 2,500-hour cumulative compute cap corresponded to a maximum wall-clock runtime of approximately 10.4 days per search (which only a few compute-intensive searches reached; most terminated earlier upon reaching 2,500 nodes). Total computational cost per ERA search depends on LLM token usage (which scales with prompt length, generated code length, and model tier) and sandbox CPU execution time. Because the prospective searches used Gemini 2.5 Flash on CPU sandboxes with a prompt scaffold similar to our prior study2, per-node LLM token usage was comparable to the values reported there (approximately 10,000 request tokens and 3,000 response tokens per node).

Within these total node and time bounds, the LLM agent generated candidate code that was executed inside a sealed evaluation harness described in the previous section; only the resulting score and execution logs were returned to the agent, with all data and evaluation logic immutable from the agent’s perspective.

For each pathogen and forecast origin, searches were initialized under one of three prompt regimes. ‘Scientist-inspired’ prompts provide the agent with a description of an existing methodology—drawn from metadata of models submitting to one of the forecasting hubs (e.g., FluSight) or summarized from a published paper—and instruct it to implement and refine that method. ‘Recombination’ prompts provide descriptions of two distinct existing methods and instruct the agent to combine their logic into a single hybrid model that encompasses the strengths of both components2. ‘AI-led’ searches receive either a method prompt generated by Gemini Deep Research or only the task description, leaving the search unconstrained over architectures.

Influenza benefited from the richest existing modeling ecosystem resulting in 56 unique prompts and modeling strategies: its prompt set spanned active FluSight and COVIDHub submissions, historically high-performing methods identified by experts from the published literature, modeling suggestions generated by Gemini Deep Research, and a structured grid of mechanistic–statistical recombinations. For COVID-19, ERA prompts primarily targeted active COVIDHub submissions, supplemented by a subset of high-performing models carried over from the prior retrospective study 2. This was the inaugural season of RSVHub, an infection that is less modeled in published literature. We used 14 prompts targeting the small number of available RSVHub methods alongside Gemini Deep Research-suggested architectures; the limited pool of viable base models precluded systematic recombination.

The canonical base prompt used as a scaffold to seed all influenza ERA runs is included in Supplementary Section 1, with infection-specific variants for COVID-19 and RSV in Supplementary Section 2. Additional specific modeling instructions provided to ERA for each method can be found in the GoogleHub repository¶¶ ¶ https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/epi_forecasts.

#### 4.2 Two-stage Model Selection

Optimization metric and moving-window aggregation. During search, candidates were scored using WIS on the validation block of the relevant pathogen-season split (Fig. 1d, purple). To avoid rewarding candidates that fit narrowly to a single forecast origin, each candidate’s validation WIS was aggregated across multiple rolling origins within the validation block. This encourages the search to select models that perform consistently across epidemic phases in a season (growth, peak, and decline). This aggregated validation WIS drove node selection within the PUCT tree search.

Post-search node selection. A single ERA search produces a tree of candidates whose aggregated validation WIS scores are known by construction. To choose one representative model per search while protecting against overfitting to the validation block, we evaluated every node post-hoc on a held-out retrospective test block (Fig. 1d, orange)—a period never seen by the agent during the search—and selected the node minimizing

$$ \text{Selection Score}=\text{Validation WIS}+2\times\text{Retrospective Test WIS}. $$

The $2\times$ weighting on the retrospective test term places greater emphasis on out-of-search generalization than on in-search fit.

### 5 Real-time Prospective Implementation

#### 5.1 Pathogen-specific Implementations

The application of ERA varied across the three target pathogens due to differences in data availability and hub maturity. Influenza benefited from a mature forecasting ecosystem, allowing for a large pool of candidate models (see Methods 4.1). For COVID-19, in addition to new ERA-generated models, five models were carried over from a retrospective study2 and fine-tuned on the larger validation dataset available for this prospective season. RSV presented a qualitatively different challenge. Historical surveillance data for this pathogen are extremely limited, the published forecasting literature is sparse, and the short available hospitalization record constrained the size of meaningful validation and test splits. To compensate, we provided ERA models with concurrent COVID-19 and influenza hospitalization time series as auxiliary inputs to harness for generalizable cross-pathogen patterns. This resulted in a comparatively smaller pool of models (see Supplementary Fig. 1).

#### 5.2 Model Selection

Initially, to construct a large library of reasonable forecasting candidates, we executed a wide array of independent ERA search experiments prior to the start of the prospective season using the prompt sources outlined in Methods 4.1. Then, the optimal ‘best node’ from each independent search tree was identified using the compound selection score (3). From this pool, a subset was curated for inclusion in GoogleHub based on a combination of their performance scores and methodological diversity. Finally, a smaller, high-performance subset was selected to form the official Google-SAI submission ensemble for each pathogen. The model selection process is outlined in Supplementary Fig. 1.

For several modeling strategies, multiple independent ERA search runs were conducted. When an initial run failed to reproduce the target methodology faithfully—as assessed by expert review—additional runs were launched with modified configurations to increase the likelihood of a faithful implementation. In some cases, a non-faithful adaptation nonetheless produced strong forecasting performance and was retained in the model pool alongside its more faithful counterparts. This accounts for the presence of multiple versions of certain models in GoogleHub and in Supplementary Tables 2, 4, 6 (indicated by version $v$ ).

We note that, for influenza, a strategy shift occurred around January 24, 2026; upon learning that the CDC utilizes log WIS rather than WIS as the primary metric for official evaluations, we updated our selection process to prioritize models based on Log WIS performance. We did not rerun ERA to search for models, rather, we calculated log WIS scores post-hoc and used these to select best models for inclusion in GoogleHub and in Google_SAI-FluEns. We examine the sensitivity of downstream forecast behavior to this choice of optimization metric in Results.

#### 5.3 Generating Prospective Forecasts and Ensembles

The prospective evaluation phase consisted of approximately 25 weeks of live submissions to the three forecasting hubs. Selected models (described in the previous section) were frozen at the season start—ERA was run once to generate each model, then the same model code was retrained each week using the real-time surveillance data released that week. Retraining models consisted solely of refitting their statistical parameters (e.g., autoregressive coefficients, regression weights) and tuning internal hyperparameters (e.g., lag lengths, window sizes) via rolling validation loops executed in the training and validation windows. Models then generated forecasts for each week’s reference date, including predictions for all four horizons and all 52 jurisdictions, which were submitted to GoogleHub weekly.

Final ensemble forecasts for all three pathogens were generated using a median ensemble approach, where the prediction for each jurisdiction and horizon was calculated as a direct quantile average of the 23 quantiles across all participating component models, still ensuring monotonicity of the outputs.

### 6 Retrospective Experiment Design

#### 6.1 Analysis of Optimization Metrics

We investigated how the choice of ERA’s internal optimization metric dictates stability of the search and the behavior of output forecasts. For each optimization metric, we conducted five independent ERA searches, yielding 15 searches in total. All searches used the same influenza forecasting task, prompt, data, and computational budget, such that only the optimization metric differed between conditions. During search, candidate nodes were scored on the validation set using the assigned optimization metric. Following search completion, all nodes from each search tree were evaluated post-hoc on the retrospective test set using the same metric, and one final node per search was selected using Equation (3), with the validation and retrospective test WIS terms replaced by the corresponding optimization metric. The resulting five selected models for each condition were then evaluated using all three metrics, allowing us to assess both performance on the metric targeted during search and performance under the alternative scoring rules.

We run ERA using three additional optimization metrics from the two principal families of proper scoring rules for probabilistic forecasting 18. First, the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) is a distance-based metric that measures the integrated squared difference between the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the forecast $F$ , and the empirical CDF of the observation $y$ . It is defined as

$$ \text{CRPS}(F,y)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(F(x)-\mathbb{1}(x\geq y))^{2}\,dx, $$

where $\mathbb{1}(x\geq y)$ is an indicator function that equals one if $x\geq y$ and zero otherwise. CRPS penalizes both over- and underprediction continuously, scaling with the absolute magnitude of the forecast error. The WIS (1) serves as a discrete approximation of this exact CRPS integral, evaluating the predictive distribution across a finite set of quantiles.

Second, Log-scale CRPS adapts this distance metric for epidemiological targets that span multiple orders of magnitude, applying greater sensitivity to relative rather than absolute errors. It is computed by applying a natural logarithm transformation to both the predictive distribution and the ground truth observation prior to scoring

$$ \text{Log-CRPS}(F_{\log},y)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(F_{\log}(x)-\mathbb{1}(x\geq\log(y)))^{2}\,dx, $$

where $F_{\log}$ represents the CDF of the log-transformed predictions. In practice, to accommodate zero-counts in incidence data, a $+1$ offset is added to both predictions and observations prior to transformation. This is the continuous analogue of log WIS.

The Logarithmic Score (Log Score) is a local proper scoring rule based on the predictive probability density or mass function, $f$ . Because the ERA evaluation harness requires a metric to be minimized (a loss function), we evaluate the negative log-probability assigned to the true observation $y$

$$ \text{Log Score}(f,y)=-\log(f(y)). $$

Unlike distance-based metrics, the Log Score evaluates only the probability mass placed exactly on the observed outcome. Consequently, if a model’s predictive distribution assigns zero probability to the ground truth outcomes, it incurs an effectively infinite penalty (as $-\log(0)\to\infty$ ), regardless of how close the bulk of the distribution falls to the observed value.

To enable the calculation of Log Scores during these optimization experiments, we modified the predictive output format. Rather than generating the standard 23 quantiles, models in this subset were required to output 1,000 predictive samples per target. This sample-based format allowed for the use of the scoringrules41 library, which provides robust implementations for Log Score, CRPS, and Log-CRPS calculations. To guarantee data integrity, all retrospective experiments were conducted using an immutable evaluation harness that isolated the LLM agent from the ground-truth data (Methods 3).

#### 6.2 Evaluation of ERA Instruction Following

We conducted a retrospective sensitivity analysis to assess how instruction-following fidelity varied with the LLM used for code generation and with the inclusion of an in-loop fidelity judge. We compared four search configurations: (1) Gemini 2.5 Flash without an in-loop judge, (2) Gemini 2.5 Flash with an in-loop judge, (3) Gemini 3 Flash without a judge, and (4) Gemini 3 Pro without a judge. The in-loop judge (itself a call to Gemini 2.5 Flash) was evaluated only with Gemini 2.5 Flash and was not crossed with the two Gemini 3 configurations.

We applied each configuration to four established FluSight methods spanning distinct modeling strategies: (1) a pure ML gradient-boosting model UMass-gbqr32, which uses feature engineering and gradient boosting; (2) a package-dependent spatial time-series model UGA_flucast-INFLAenza16; (3) a hierarchical compartmental model Cornell_JHU-hierarchSIR1; and (4) a probability-generating-function-based model NU-PGF_FLUH39. Each method was used as the target for each of the four ERA configurations described above. Three independent search trajectories were conducted for each configuration–method combination under matched computational budgets, giving 48 searches in total.

All searches were subject to the same stopping criteria. A search terminated after either 2,500 explored nodes or 2,500 cumulative hours of parallel sandbox runtime, whichever occurred first. These dual criteria bounded both the breadth of the search and the computational time available to models with different runtime requirements. Within each trajectory, the final model was selected according to the selection score defined in Equation (3).

For the configuration incorporating an in-loop judge, Gemini 2.5 Flash was used both to generate code and, through a separate and independent API call, to assess fidelity. After code had been generated at each node, the judge received the method-specific seed instruction together with the candidate model code (Supplementary Section D). It then assigned an instruction-fidelity score from one to ten. Candidate implementations meeting the prespecified threshold of seven proceeded to full validation and received a validation-based score. Candidates below the threshold were not validated and were instead assigned a penalty value of 1,000 when calculating the in-search validation WIS. The judge therefore acted as a binary gate within the otherwise single-objective search, preventing candidates assessed as non-compliant from advancing on the basis of predictive performance alone.

After search completion, the selected model from every trajectory was evaluated by the same external post-search judge. Unlike the generic in-loop judge, the external judge used a method-specific rubric developed by an expert epidemiologist (N.G.R.). Each rubric identified the principal features required for the generated code to constitute a faithful implementation of the corresponding reference method. On the basis of the generated code and this rubric, the external judge classified each implementation as a ‘Match,’ ‘Partial Match,’ or ‘No Match.’ This post-search assessment did not affect model selection and was used only to evaluate the methodological fidelity of the selected models.

We assessed concordance between the external judge and independent classifications made by N.G.R. on a subset of ten retrospectively generated models. The classifications agreed in all but one case. In the discordant case, the generated code nominally implemented the requested method in a try block but fell back to degenerate output via an except clause, which the judge assessed as compliant based on the code structure alone. This case identified a limitation of code-only fidelity assessment when the implemented fallback behavior differs from the apparent primary implementation.
